subject: sunglasses
title: What If You Never Wore Sunglasses?

scenes.text: What if you never wore sunglasses? Your eyes would keep a tally you can't feel.
One sunny day on fresh snow, which bounces back up to 80 percent of UV, can sunburn your corneas.
That's snow blindness. It's painful, and symptoms can last up to two days before they fade.
By your teens or twenties, years of glare can grow surfer's eye, a fleshy film creeping onto the cornea.
Decades later, UV clouds the lens. The WHO links about one in ten cases of cataract blindness to sunlight.
And over a lifetime, the thin skin of your eyelids can grow the same cancers as a sunburned nose.

description:
What if you never wore sunglasses? Fresh snow reflects up to about 80 percent of UV and can burn the cornea (photokeratitis, or snow blindness), with symptoms lasting up to about two days. Long hours in the sun can cause pterygium, surfer's eye, even in the teens or twenties.
The WHO estimates roughly 10 percent of cataract blindness may be due to UV exposure, and UV is linked to basal and squamous cell cancers of the eyelid. Not medical advice.
